record.paper_title: Ductile-to-brittle transition and yielding in soft amorphous materials: perspectives and open questions
record.original_question: What length scales are associated with memory formation in jammed materials and gels, and how can X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy or multispeckle dynamic light scattering link those length scales to memory storage and the yielding transition across soft glasses and gels?

evidence.quote: These results raise the question of length scales associated with memory formation in jammed materials and gels. In practice, such a length scale could be determined experimentally via X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy (XPCS), 166 or multispeckle dynamics light scattering, 167 which calls for a more systematic use of these techniques to investigate the yielding transition in various types of soft solids, from soft glasses to gels, in order to link their respective length scale to memory storage.

artifact.category_tag: soft amorphous materials and rheological memory
artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider soft amorphous solids — including jammed suspensions, soft glasses, and colloidal or polymer gels — that, when subjected to cyclic or transient shear deformations below or near their yielding transition, can encode and retain a memory of the imposed strain amplitude or stress history. By "memory" one means a measurable observable (for example, a feature in the stress response or in microstructural correlations) that allows the previously imposed driving conditions to be read out at a later time.

Assume one can perform space- and time-resolved measurements of the microscopic dynamics of such a material via techniques capable of probing particle rearrangements at wavevectors q (e.g., intensity autocorrelation functions g_2(q,t) and their multi-time generalizations), so that a correlation length ξ_mem(q,t;γ) characterizing spatial coherence of rearrangements during and after a training protocol of amplitude γ can be extracted.

Problems:
(a) Define precisely, in terms of two-time or four-point dynamic correlation functions of the microscopic density (or particle displacement field), a correlation length ξ_mem associated with memory formation in jammed materials and in gels, and establish its existence and finiteness as a function of training amplitude γ relative to the yield strain γ_Y.
(b) Determine the scaling behavior of ξ_mem as γ → γ_Y from below in (i) jammed soft-glass systems and (ii) attractive gel networks, and identify whether ξ_mem diverges, saturates, or develops a characteristic non-monotonic dependence at the yielding transition.
(c) Establish a quantitative relation linking ξ_mem to the capacity of the material to store memory (number of independently retrievable memories and their fidelity), and contrast the resulting length scale for soft glasses with that for gels.
artifact.status_search_result: The question is posed as an open research direction concerning length scales of rheological memory formation across soft glasses and gels. Recent literature on memory in matter (Keim et al. review, Rev. Mod. Phys. 2019) and XPCS/MSDLS studies of yielding (e.g., Cipelletti and collaborators) report progress on detecting heterogeneous dynamics near yielding, but no general theory or experimental consensus identifies a memory length scale and links it systematically to the yielding transition across soft glasses and gels. The problem appears to remain open.

status_evidence.title: Memory formation in matter (Rev. Mod. Phys.)
status_evidence.snippet: Reviews memory effects in disordered and amorphous solids, noting that the spatial structure and length scales of memory remain incompletely characterized.
status_evidence.claim: Length scales of memory formation in amorphous solids are an active and open topic.

status_evidence.title: XPCS studies of yielding in soft glasses
status_evidence.snippet: X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy reveals heterogeneous dynamics near yielding but does not yet provide a unified memory length scale linking soft glasses and gels.
status_evidence.claim: Experimental link between XPCS-measured length scales and memory storage at yielding has not been established systematically.
